  Penalized function-on-function regression, as implemented in the R package refund, considers all
  grid values as independent conditional on the linear predictor, but some dependence typically remains.

# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Function-on-function regression relates a functional response $Y_i(t)$ to functional and scalar
covariates [@RamsaySilverman2005; @MullerYao2008; @Morris2015]. Its terms can include, amongst others, a *functional intercept* $\alpha(t)$, the linear predictor at zero covariates; *coefficient surfaces* $\beta(s,t)$ for functional covariates, which weight the covariate's value at position $s$ in its effect on the
response at $t$; and *coefficient functions* $\gamma(t)$ for $t$-varying effects of scalar covariates. In the penalized
framework of @IvanescuStaicuScheiplGreven2015 and @GrevenScheipl2017, implemented in `pffr()` of the
R package refund [@ScheiplStaicuGreven2015; @Rpkg_refund], each term is a penalized (tensor product) spline. The model is fitted as one generalized additive model [@Wood2017] to the $N = GD$ stacked grid values of $G$
curves with $D$ points each, and the fit treats these $N$ values as independent given the additive predictor.

Real world residual curves typically violate this assumption: they tend to be somewhat smooth deviations from the mean, or artefacts of misaligned features or slow drift, so values at grid points of each curve are correlated. This dependence has two consequences.
First, smoothing-parameter selection by restricted maximum likelihood (REML),
like other data-driven selection under correlated errors [@OpsomerWangYang2001], undersmooths: the
estimates, in particular of the coefficient surface, are more variable than necessary. Second, the
model-based standard errors count $N$ independent observations although the data carry much less information. Estimated intervals are then too narrow, and finer $t$-grids make them narrower without adding information.

This paper provides guidance on what users of `pffr()` (or other functional regression software) should report, and lays out the rationale for the defaults we have implemented. Analysts who fit such a model require estimates that show the shape of each effect faithfully and intervals whose error rates are close to nominal even under strong dependence or variance heterogeneity. We evaluate the available fits and covariances
against both requirements, for Gaussian, count and binary responses, in a simulation with `r n_cells`
settings and in a plasmode study that attaches the real residual curves of nine datasets to known
"truths".

Curve-blocked neighborhood cross-validation (NCV) [@Wood2024] chooses the smoothing parameters by leaving out one
whole curve at a time. In the simulation's main settings, REML's relative error for $\beta(s,t)$ under dependence is two to four times that of this NCV fit. The gap grows on denser grids and
with larger bases, and shrinks with a rough truth and under misregistration of the responses. When the true $\beta(s,t)$ is
zero and the errors are smooth, REML's estimate shows spurious structure, and NCV's stays much closer
to zero.

On the plasmode data, the error of either fit for $\beta(s,t)$ is large relative to the effect. A possible
reason is weak identification: in directions that the functional covariate does not vary in, $\beta(s,t)$ is free to vary with hardly any effect on the fitted values [@ScheiplGreven2016].\\
NCV estimates the surface better for most "truths" on most datasets, but not always: it is worse on some datasets when the "truth" is rough.

Under dependence, model-based intervals are far too narrow for fitted means and model terms, both in the simulation and on real residual curves, and coverage of $\beta(s,t)$ falls further on denser grids.

A curve-clustered sandwich covariance with a leverage adjustment for the penalized hat matrix (CL2),
computed after the usual REML fit (REML + CL2), brings coverage of fitted means and $\beta(s,t)$ close to
nominal in the simulation's main settings. On the real residual curves of the plasmode study, it falls a few
percentage points short on eight of nine datasets but Satterthwaite degrees of freedom recover most of the remaining shortfall at the cost of
wider intervals. In the simulation, they do so also with 20 curves, and with 40 or 100 curves they keep the
pointwise false-positive rate for a zero surface close to nominal under smooth errors.

Neither the REML nor the NCV fit gave both a good estimate and calibrated intervals for the surface.
REML + CL2 intervals are wide because REML's estimate is noisy. Intervals centered at the NCV estimate
are narrow but undercover. In the simulation, the cause is smoothing bias; on the plasmode data the
diagnostics suggest smoothing bias and the variability of the selected smoothing parameters. The
corrections we tried did not calibrate these intervals on the plasmode data.

These results show the classical tension between estimation and pointwise inference in nonparametric
regression. An undersmoothed estimate has small bias relative to its standard error, so its
intervals can hold their level; an estimate smoothed for accuracy needs an explicit bias correction,
whose own variability then enters the interval [@Hall1992; @CalonicoCattaneoFarrell2018]. Here REML
undersmooths through the dependence rather than by design, and in the simulation its intervals with
CL2 cover.

The tension is strongest for effects that vary along $t$ and a second argument. For a smooth effect of
a scalar covariate that varies along $t$, REML's error still exceeds NCV's, but by less. In the main
settings the two fits estimate the functional intercept and the coefficient functions of scalar covariates
about equally well, and NCV estimates fitted means modestly better. For these three, REML + CL2 gives both
a good estimate and intervals close to nominal, except for the intercepts and coefficient functions of
binary responses and for counts under misregistration.

Our recommendation therefore depends on the goal, which in practice may mean fitting the model twice
(@sec-recommend). To learn the shape of a $\beta(s,t)$ surface, use curve-blocked NCV, our default, which typically smooths more
than REML. For inference about that surface, use REML + CL2 with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.

We make four contributions. (i) We give evidence on how much curve-blocked NCV improves the estimate of
the coefficient surface over REML, and where it does not. (ii) We compute the CR2 leverage adjustment of
@BellMcCaffrey2002 with the non-idempotent hat matrix of penalized fits, combine it with the model-based
smoothing-bias allowance and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, and implement it in the refund R package.
(iii) Our evaluation reports estimation error, width, detection of non-zero effects
and false detections of a zero effect next to coverage, in synthetic and real-data-based settings of varying sizes and noisiness.
(iv) We report negative results on intervals centered at the NCV estimate and on other attempted
remedies in the supplement.

*Related work.* Within-curve dependence can be modeled directly: by functional mixed models with
structured residual covariance [@MorrisCarroll2006; @MeyerCoullVersaceCinciripiniMorris2015], by
generalized least squares with an estimated residual covariance [@ReissHuangMennes2010] and by
curve-level functional random effects [@ScheiplGertheissGreven2016]; the last two underlie two of our
comparators. Signal compression [@LuoQi2017] is a different estimator of the coefficient surface.
Correlated errors distort data-driven selection in scalar smoothing [@OpsomerWangYang2001;
@CaronParteDedeckerMichel2026]; likelihood-based selection is less sensitive than generalized
cross-validation [@KrivobokovaKauermann2007]. Leaving out whole curves avoids modeling the
dependence [@RiceSilverman1991], and neighborhood cross-validation [@Wood2024] makes this cheap.

For inference, pointwise and simultaneous bands for functional means and for function-on-scalar and
scalar-on-function models are well developed [@Degras2011; @GoldsmithGrevenCrainiceanu2013;
@ChoiReimherr2018; @LieblReimherr2023]. Fast univariate inference
[@CuiLerouxSmirnovaCrainiceanu2022] and penalized functional generalized estimating equations
[@LoewingerLevisCuiPereira2025] address longitudinal functional data with many subjects.
Working-independence estimators for clustered data are consistent but can be inefficient
[@LinCarroll2000; @WelshLinCarroll2002]. Cluster-robust covariances need only independence across
clusters [@LiangZeger1986; @CameronMiller2015; @ZeileisKoellGraham2020; @HansenLee2019]. With few
clusters the leverage adjustment of @BellMcCaffrey2002 and its extensions [@McCaffreyBell2006;
@PustejovskyTipton2018] reduce the downward bias of the sandwich [@KauermannCarroll2001]. Here the
number of coefficients (about 100) is comparable to the number of curves, so per-curve leverage is not
negligible [@MacKinnonNielsenWebb2023guide; @CarterSchnepelSteigerwald2017]. @Korolev2026 adjusts the
cluster-robust covariance for the penalty in semiparametric panel models fitted with mgcv.

# Model, fits and covariances {#sec-model}

## Model and penalized fit

We work within the general functional regression framework of @GrevenScheipl2017, which relates a
feature of the conditional distribution of a functional response $Y_i(t)$ given covariate set $\mathcal X_i$ to an
additive predictor,
$$
\boldsymbol\xi(Y_i(t) \mid \mathcal X_i) = h(\mathcal X_i) = \sum_{\ell=1}^{L} h_\ell(\mathcal X_i).
$$ {#eq-gfamm}
The response is a function $Y_i(t)$ over an interval $\mathcal T$, with scalar responses as the
special case of a single-point $\mathcal T$, and $\mathcal X_i$ can contain scalar and
square-integrable functional covariates as well as grouping factors. The transformation
$\boldsymbol\xi$ determines the modeled feature: for generalized functional
additive mixed models (GFAMMs) [@ScheiplGertheissGreven2016], the pointwise conditional mean under a
link function, $\boldsymbol\xi = g \circ \mathrm E$. Each partial predictor $h_\ell(\mathcal X_i)$ is
a function over $\mathcal T$ with values $h_\ell(\mathcal X_i)(t)$ and depends on a subset of the
covariates. Options include functional intercepts, linear or smooth effects of scalar and functional
covariates, their interactions, and functional random effects, in which case the model also
conditions on these latent processes.

In the following, we use a GFAMM with three partial predictors and no functional random effects. For curves
$i = 1, \dots, G$ observed at $t_1, \dots, t_D$, the model is
$$
g\{\mathrm{E}[Y_i(t) \mid X_i, v_i]\} = \eta_i(t) = \alpha(t) + \int_{\mathcal S} X_i(s)\,\beta(s,t)\,ds + v_i\,\gamma(t),
$$ {#eq-model}
with link $g$, functional intercept $\alpha(t)$, coefficient surface $\beta(s,t)$ of the
functional covariate $X_i(s)$ and coefficient function $\gamma(t)$ of the scalar covariate $v_i$. A
smooth effect $f(x_i, t)$ of a scalar covariate can replace the functional term. The responses
follow an exponential family, or an "extended" family such as the scaled $t$-distribution [@WoodPyaSafken2016], with mean
$g^{-1}\{\eta_i(t)\}$ and variance $\phi V(\mu)$.

Each term is expanded in a penalized spline basis, with tensor product splines for multivariate terms.
The stacked predictor is $\boldsymbol\eta = \mathbf X\boldsymbol\theta$ with penalty
$\sum_r \lambda_r \boldsymbol\theta^\top \mathbf S_r \boldsymbol\theta$. Penalized iteratively
reweighted least squares gives $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ for given smoothing parameters
$\boldsymbol\lambda$. Let $\mathbf W$ be the diagonal matrix of working weights
$(d\mu/d\eta)^2/\{\phi V(\mu)\}$ at convergence and $\mathbf S = \sum_r (\lambda_r/\phi)\mathbf S_r$.
The Bayesian and the frequentist covariance under the working model are
$$
\mathbf V_p = (\mathbf X^\top \mathbf W \mathbf X + \mathbf S)^{-1}, \qquad
\mathbf V_e = \mathbf V_p \mathbf X^\top \mathbf W \mathbf X\, \mathbf V_p .
$$ {#eq-vp}
Their difference $\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e = \mathbf V_p \mathbf S \mathbf V_p$ is a
prior-averaged allowance for smoothing bias [@Wahba1983; @Nychka1988; @MarraWood2012]. For REML
fits mgcv adds a term for the uncertainty of $\hat{\boldsymbol\lambda}$ and returns $\mathbf V_c$
[@WoodPyaSafken2016]. The *model-based* intervals below use $\mathbf V_c$ for REML fits and
$\mathbf V_p$ for NCV fits, because the $\mathbf V_c$ that mgcv returns for NCV fits in the version
used here is not a valid covariance (Supplement S6). The two model-based intervals therefore contain
different uncertainty terms. All these covariances assume that all $N$ values $Y_i(t_j)$ are conditionally independent given $\mathcal X_i$.

## Smoothing-parameter selection

*REML* maximizes the Laplace-approximate restricted likelihood of the working model [@Wood2011].
Estimating a term averages residual curves with weights that depend on the covariates. Within a curve,
neighboring residuals are correlated, so pooling across grid points reduces the noise in this average
much less than assumed by the working likelihood, which counts $N$ independent values. We believe this excess
noise, to the extent that the chosen spline basis can represent it, is picked up as signal by REML when it selects too little
smoothing. REML's excess error grows under dependence and on denser grids (@sec-res-estimation), which fits
this reading.

*Curve-blocked NCV.* Neighborhood cross-validation [@Wood2024] minimizes
$$
\mathcal C(\boldsymbol\lambda) = \sum_{k=1}^{m}\sum_{(i,j)\in \mathcal N_k} \mathrm{dev}\bigl(y_{ij}, \hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-\mathcal N_k}_{\boldsymbol\lambda}\bigr),
$$ {#eq-ncv}
the deviance of predictions for the points in $\mathcal N_k$ from the fit without them, with
$y_{ij} = Y_i(t_j)$. We use one neighborhood per curve, $\mathcal N_k = \{(k,j): j = 1, \dots, D\}$, so
$m = G$ and each neighborhood has as many points as its curve. The criterion then measures how well a fit to the other curves predicts a new
curve from its covariates [@RiceSilverman1991]. If residual curves are independent across curves, no information about the left-out curve is contained in the noise
a fit follows in the other curves, so following its pattern worsens predictions and the criterion selects stronger smoothing even without an explicit model of the dependence. This holds only for the modes of variation of a term that directly affects predictions, i.e., not for changes such as $\beta(s,t) + \delta(s)f(t)$ with $\delta(s)$ in the kernel of the covariance operator of $X(s)$ [@ScheiplGreven2016].
Where curves are dependent on each other, the neighborhoods
should be sub-groups that are independent of each other, such as all curves of a given subject. Spatial block neighborhoods
are evaluated on the three datasets with dependent source curves (Supplement S2.3); subject neighborhoods
were not evaluated in this work.

No curve is actually refitted: $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}^{-\mathcal N_k}$ is approximated by a single Newton
step based on the full fit (so: exact only for Gaussian responses with identity link and given $\boldsymbol\lambda$), and $\mathcal C$ is minimized over $\boldsymbol\lambda$ with analytic
derivatives [@Wood2024]. Gaussian fits with $G = 100$ and $D = 61$ using curve-blocked NCV took a median
`r f(med_time("NCV"), 1)` s against `r f(med_time("REML"), 1)` s for REML.

## Curve-clustered covariances {#sec-cl2}

The curve-clustered sandwich replaces the variance part of $\mathbf V_p$ by one
that does not assume conditional independence within curves. It does assume conditional independence across curves as well as a correct model for the mean. Write $\tilde{\mathbf X}_i = \mathbf W_i^{1/2}\mathbf X_i$ for the weighted
design rows of curve $i$, $\mathbf z_i$ for its Pearson residuals, and
$\tilde{\mathbf H} = \tilde{\mathbf X}\mathbf V_p\tilde{\mathbf X}^\top$ for the penalized hat
matrix. The CL2 covariance is
$$
\hat{\mathbf V}_{\mathrm{CL2}} = \frac{G}{G-1}\,\mathbf V_p \Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^G \mathbf U_i \mathbf U_i^\top\Bigr) \mathbf V_p + (\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e),
\qquad
\mathbf U_i = \tilde{\mathbf X}_i^\top \mathbf R_i^{-1/2}\mathbf z_i ,
$$ {#eq-cl2}
with $\mathbf R_i = [(\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H})(\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H})^\top]_{ii}$,
the block of curve $i$ in the covariance of the residuals under the working model. CR1, the
usual cluster-robust covariance [@LiangZeger1986], sets $\mathbf R_i = \mathbf I$. The adjustment
$\mathbf R_i^{-1/2}$ is the bias-reduced linearization of @BellMcCaffrey2002 (CR2), with the
penalized hat in place of a projection. Because $\tilde{\mathbf H}$ is not idempotent,
$\mathbf R_i \neq \mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H}_{ii}$; the full block is computed. We keep the
factor $G/(G-1)$, floor the eigenvalues of $\mathbf R_i$ at $10^{-6}$, and write CL2 to mark
these departures from CR2. The second term of @eq-cl2 keeps the model-based allowance for smoothing
bias, so CL2 replaces only the variance part of $\mathbf V_p$. The variance part estimates the
sampling variance of $\hat{\boldsymbol\theta}$ around its penalized target; the added
$\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e$ is a prior-averaged allowance for the distance between that target and
the truth which does not provide guaranteed coverage of every fixed truth (Appendix A.3).

The sandwich must use the penalized bread $\mathbf V_p$ and the penalized hat. General-purpose
cluster-robust software uses the unpenalized hat or bread and returns invalid covariances for
penalized fits [@Rpkg_sandwich; @Rpkg_clubSandwich]. Limited asymptotic consistency and validity results for fixed smoothing parameters are provided in Appendix A.5, but in the realistic regimes we study here (about as many spline coefficients as curves, non-negligible penalties and estimated smoothing parameters), the required assumptions do not apply.
CL2 is a finite-sample procedure whose behavior is established empirically below.

*Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.* For any contrast $\mathbf a^\top\boldsymbol\theta$, the variance
part of @eq-cl2 is a sum of squares $\sum_i (\mathbf q_i^\top\mathbf z_i)^2$ with
$\mathbf q_i = \mathbf R_i^{-1/2}\tilde{\mathbf X}_i\mathbf V_p\mathbf a$, up to the factor
$G/(G-1)$. Under a Gaussian working model with fixed $\boldsymbol\lambda$ and no smoothing bias, the residuals are $(\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H})\boldsymbol\varepsilon$ with independent standard normal $\boldsymbol\varepsilon$, and matching the first two moments of the quadratic form to a scaled
$\chi^2_\nu$ gives $\nu = (\operatorname{tr}\boldsymbol\Gamma)^2/\operatorname{tr}(\boldsymbol\Gamma^2)$
with
$\Gamma_{ih} = \mathbf q_i^\top[(\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H})(\mathbf I - \tilde{\mathbf H})^\top]_{ih}\mathbf q_h$
[see Appendix A.7 and @BellMcCaffrey2002; @PustejovskyTipton2018]. The interval uses the $t_\nu$ quantile at
each grid point. We use the same $\nu$ for all families (Appendix A.7 discusses this choice). The degrees of freedom ignore non-normality of the responses, the bias allowance, the dependence and the selection of $\boldsymbol\lambda$; they are a reference distribution, not an exact pivot.

The same constructions apply to both fits: *REML + CL2* is @eq-cl2 at the REML estimate and
*NCV + CL2* at the NCV estimate.

## Estimands and performance measures {#sec-measures}

Four estimands are evaluated on fixed grids: the conditional mean $\mathrm E(Y \mid X)$ for a fixed
set of 50 subjects' covariates, on the response scale; $\beta(s,t)$ (or $f(x,t)$); $\alpha(t)$;
and $\gamma(t)$, on the link scale. Pointwise intervals are estimate $\pm$ critical value $\times$
standard error, transformed by $g^{-1}$ for the mean. Every method is judged on accuracy of the
estimate, calibration and informativeness [@MorrisWhiteCrowther2019]:

- *Coverage*: the share of replicates whose interval contains the truth at a grid point, averaged
  over the grid. Its Monte Carlo standard error is the standard deviation over replicates of the
  grid-averaged coverage divided by the square root of the number of replicates. The *lower tail*
  is the 5% quantile of pointwise coverage over the grid.
- *Relative error*: $\{\sum_j(\hat\vartheta_j - \vartheta_j)^2/\sum_j\tilde\vartheta_j^2\}^{1/2}$ over
  grid points $j$, for estimate $\hat\vartheta$ and truth $\vartheta$, with $\tilde\vartheta = \vartheta$
  for $\beta$ and $\gamma$ and $\tilde\vartheta$ the truth centered at its grid mean for the mean and
  $\alpha(t)$, whose level is not the effect. A value of 1 means the error is as large as the
  effect. We report its median over replicates.
- *Relative half-width*: the root-mean-square half-width of the intervals over the grid, divided by
  $(\sum_j\tilde\vartheta_j^2/D)^{1/2}$, the root-mean-square size of the (centered) truth.
- *Detection rate*: among grid points where the absolute true value exceeds 25% of its maximum,
  $|\vartheta_j| > 0.25\max_k|\vartheta_k|$, the share whose interval excludes zero on the side of
  the truth.
- *Interval score* [@GneitingRaftery2007]: for an interval $[l, u]$ and true value $\vartheta$,
  $(u - l) + (2/0.05)\{(l - \vartheta)_+ + (\vartheta - u)_+\}$, averaged over the grid and the
  replicates; lower is better. It is a proper scoring rule for predictive quantile intervals;
  against fixed truths over repeated datasets it rewards an accurate center and a narrow width
  together and is not a calibration criterion. We report it relative to REML + CL2 and interpret it in context of
  the other measures.

The supplement adds wrong-sign rates and studentized errors. Comparisons of estimators use the
relative error; where ratios of mean squared errors are given, they are labeled as such.
@tbl-constructions lists the principal interval constructions and where each was evaluated.

# Simulation design {#sec-design}

The simulation follows the model in @eq-model with a functional covariate whose spectrum matches the
corpus-callosum profiles of the DTI data in refund (`r n_cells` settings, `r n_rep` replicates
each, `r format(n_tasks, big.mark = ",")` fits per selector; Appendix B.1 lists all blocks of
settings). The truths
are fixed smooth functions, projected onto the used spline bases so that they are representable without error;
"rough" variants add higher-frequency components. Responses are Gaussian (signal-to-noise
$R^2 = 0.2, 0.5, 0.8$), Poisson and Bernoulli at each grid point (two signal-to-noise levels on the link
scale), with scaled $t$, Beta and Negative-Binomial responses as extensions.

Within-curve errors
are zero-mean processes with correlation kernel $R$, used directly for Gaussian responses and as the
latent layer of a Gaussian copula otherwise, so that every marginal remains in the fitted family.
So for count and binary data, the dependence is a copula construction, and the support for
CL2 with these families is empirical within that construction. Three error processes form the main
factorial:

- *independent*: $R(t,t') = \mathbb 1\{t = t'\}$;
- *rough stationary*: $R(t,t') = 0.8\exp(-|t-t'|/0.089) + 0.2\,\mathbb 1\{t=t'\}$;
- *smooth non-stationary*: the residual correlation of the DTI regression in refund (@fig-kernels in Appendix B.1).

The main factorial crosses these processes with the family, $G \in \{40, 100\}$ and the signal
level at $D = 61$ grid points. Extensions vary one factor at a time: the main factorial with
$G = 20$, a four times denser grid, a rough truth, a coefficient surface that is zero everywhere
($\beta \equiv 0$; Gaussian and binary responses, independent and smooth errors), a smooth effect $f(x,t)$ in place of the functional term $\int X(s)\beta(s,t) ds$, sign-changing and
heteroskedastic errors, misregistration (each curve observed on its own clock / deformed elastically), a low-rank functional covariate and larger bases.

The fitted bases are cubic B-splines with first-order
difference penalties (mgcv's `ps` basis with `m = c(2, 1)`), so the penalty null space contains the
constants along each direction: $k = 12$ along $t$ for $\alpha(t)$ and $\gamma(t)$ and an $8 \times 10$
tensor product for $\beta(s,t)$, about 100 coefficients in total; the larger bases halve and quarter the
knot spacing. Results with second-order penalties were not computed.

Each replicate is fitted by REML and by curve-blocked NCV, none of the fits failed. For NCV fits
of scaled-$t$ responses, mgcv often reported that the search over the smoothing parameters ended without
meeting its convergence test (`r f(100 * cflag_rate("fpc"), 0)`% under smooth errors,
`r f(100 * cflag_rate("iid"), 0)`% under independent errors, but results were mostly stable under refits from different starting values indicating flat optima), and rarely in other families; REML fits
were not affected (settings with at least 40 curves and a non-zero surface; Appendix B.1). Random draws depend
only on the replicate, so contrasts between methods and settings are paired. The Monte Carlo standard
error of a grid-averaged coverage is `r rng_pp(se_dep_cl2, 2)` (percentage points) for REML + CL2 in the dependent main-factorial settings with 100 curves.

## Estimation: REML versus NCV {#sec-res-estimation}

Under independent errors, both selectors estimate $\beta$ well: median relative error
`r f(rs("beta", "independent", "reml_cl2", "rel"), 2)` (REML) and
`r f(rs("beta", "independent", "ncv_cl2", "rel"), 2)` (NCV) over the settings. Under dependence
REML's error rises to `r f(rs("beta", "dependent", "reml_cl2", "rel"), 2)` (maximum
`r f(rs("beta", "dependent", "reml_cl2", "rel_max"), 1)`), NCV's to
factorial, the median RMSE ratio of the two (REML to NCV) is `r rng(rr(TRUE), 1)` under dependence and `r rng(rr(FALSE), 1)`
under independence, at every signal level; with 20 curves it is `r rng(rr20(TRUE), 1)` and
`r rng(rr20(FALSE), 1)`. On a four times denser grid, it reaches `r rng(rr_block("dense_grid"), 1)` and with
the larger bases `r rng(rr_block("basis_size"), 1)`; it is smaller with a rough truth
(`r rng(rr_block("rough_truth"), 1)`) and under misregistration (`r rng(rr_block("warp"), 1)`). For a smooth effect $f(x,t)$ in place of the functional term, it is `r rng(rr_est("f"), 1)`. NCV estimates $\beta$ better also under independent
Gaussian errors (ratio of mean squared errors NCV/REML `r rng(beta_ratio_iid_gau)`), so part of the gap reflects the
smooth truths rather than the dependence.

REML's surface uses `r rng(er(TRUE), 1)` times NCV's
effective degrees of freedom (EDF) under dependence (`r rng(er(FALSE), 1)` under independence). Its
excess error is variance, not bias: squared bias is `r rng(bshare("REML", "smooth"))` of REML's mean
squared error for $\beta$ and `r rng(bshare("NCV", "smooth"))` of NCV's (100 curves, smooth truth).
Larger bases make it worse: with the largest basis, REML's surface EDF under smooth errors grows
from `r rng(ed("REML", "default"), 0)` to `r rng(ed("REML", "xlarge"), 0)` across families, NCV's
from `r rng(ed("NCV", "default"), 0)` to `r rng(ed("NCV", "xlarge"), 0)` (Supplement S5).

Estimates for the mean, the intercept and the scalar effect depend much less strongly on the selector. Under independent
errors, the median relative error over the settings is `r f(rs("mean", "independent", "reml_cl2", "rel"), 2)` (REML) and
`r f(rs("mean", "independent", "ncv_cl2", "rel"), 2)` (NCV) for the mean,
`r f(rs("alpha", "independent", "reml_cl2", "rel"), 2)` and `r f(rs("alpha", "independent", "ncv_cl2", "rel"), 2)` for $\alpha(t)$, and
`r f(rs("gamma", "independent", "reml_cl2", "rel"), 2)` and `r f(rs("gamma", "independent", "ncv_cl2", "rel"), 2)` for $\gamma(t)$. Under dependence, it is
`r f(rs("mean", "dependent", "reml_cl2", "rel"), 2)` and `r f(rs("mean", "dependent", "ncv_cl2", "rel"), 2)`,
`r f(rs("alpha", "dependent", "reml_cl2", "rel"), 2)` and `r f(rs("alpha", "dependent", "ncv_cl2", "rel"), 2)`, and
`r f(rs("gamma", "dependent", "reml_cl2", "rel"), 2)` and `r f(rs("gamma", "dependent", "ncv_cl2", "rel"), 2)`
(@fig-tradeoff-summary). In the dependent main-factorial settings, the median RMSE ratio of REML to NCV is
`r rng(rr_est("mean"), 1)` for the mean, `r rng(rr_est("alpha"), 2)` for $\alpha(t)$ and `r rng(rr_est("gamma"), 2)` for $\gamma(t)$,
against `r rng(rr(TRUE), 1)` for $\beta$. NCV thus gains modestly for the mean (ratio of mean squared
errors NCV/REML `r rng(mean_ratio_dep)` with 100 curves) and little for the other two terms; for
$\alpha(t)$ the ratio stays at or below `r f(max(rr_est("alpha", fam = c("gaussian", "poisson"))), 2)` outside binary responses. REML also has the
heavier tail: `r f(100 * rs("mean", "dependent", "reml_cl2", "gt1"), 1)`% of replicates have a relative error above 1 for the mean, against
`r f(100 * rs("mean", "dependent", "ncv_cl2", "gt1"), 1)`% for NCV, with smaller differences for $\alpha(t)$
(`r f(100 * rs("alpha", "dependent", "reml_cl2", "gt1"), 1)`% and `r f(100 * rs("alpha", "dependent", "ncv_cl2", "gt1"), 1)`%) and $\gamma(t)$
(`r f(100 * rs("gamma", "dependent", "reml_cl2", "gt1"), 1)`% and `r f(100 * rs("gamma", "dependent", "ncv_cl2", "gt1"), 1)`%).

*Stability of the smoothing parameters.* GCV can have multiple minima and more variable smoothing
parameters than REML [@ReissOgden2009], and prediction-error criteria occasionally undersmooth
severely [@Wood2011]. Curve-blocked NCV, which these results do not cover, shows a similar tail. With
40 or 100 curves (Appendix B.1), the first of the surface's two smoothing parameters fell more than a
factor of $e^3 \approx 20$ below its setting's median in `r f(100 * lowsm("share_low", "independent"), 1)`% of NCV fits and in no REML fit under
independent errors, and REML estimated the surface better on `r f(100 * (1 - lowsm("ncv_beats_reml_low", "independent")), 0)`% of those replicates.
Such fits made up `r f(100 * lowsm("share_low"), 1)`% of NCV fits under dependence, apart from misregistration, but there NCV still
estimated the surface better on `r f(100 * lowsm("ncv_beats_reml_low"), 0)`% of those replicates. They have `r f(lowsm("within_ncv_low"), 1)` times their setting's
median relative error and account for `r f(100 * lowsm("mse_share_ncv_low"), 0)`% of NCV's squared error, but they do not explain its
undercoverage: leaving them out moves NCV + CL2 only from `r f(lowsm("cov_ncv_all"), 3)` to `r f(lowsm("cov_ncv_other"), 3)`. Convergence flags do
not detect them: outside scaled-$t$ responses, only `r lowsm_flag$f` of `r lowsm_flag$n` was flagged.

Neither fit is uniformly the more stable
under dependence: the median standard deviations of the two log smoothing parameters over replicates are
`r f(lowsm("sd_ncv"), 2)` and `r f(lowsm("sd2_ncv"), 2)` for NCV and `r f(lowsm("sd_reml"), 2)` and `r f(lowsm("sd2_reml"), 2)` for REML (under independence, `r f(lowsm("sd_ncv", "independent"), 2)` and
`r f(lowsm("sd2_ncv", "independent"), 2)` against `r f(lowsm("sd_reml", "independent"), 2)` and `r f(lowsm("sd2_reml", "independent"), 2)`). Restarts of flagged scaled-$t$ fits can sometimes result in materially different fits
(Appendix B.1); multiple starts were not evaluated as a fitting procedure.

*Alternative fits that smooth more.* Explicit models for the residual dependence also reduce REML's surface estimation error. Two such methods were compared with NCV on the same data, in `r n_cmp_dep` Gaussian
main-factorial settings with dependent errors and 12 plasmode combinations (Supplement S3.2): a
functional random effect for each curve based on the eigenfunctions of the REML-estimated residual curves (`pcre()` in refund), and generalized least squares (GLS) with a residual covariance estimated from the REML
residual curves by functional principal components (FPCA) plus white noise. Their mean squared error
for $\beta$, relative to NCV's (geometric mean over settings), is `r f(cmg("pcre", "dependent"), 2)`
(pcre) and `r f(cmg("gls_fpc", "dependent"), 2)` (GLS) in the simulation, where REML's is
`r f(cmg("reml_cl2", "dependent"), 1)`, and `r f(cmg("pcre", "plasmode"), 2)` and
`r f(cmg("gls_fpc", "plasmode"), 2)` on the plasmode data (midpoint truth, defined in
@sec-plasmode, with REML residuals; the GLS covariance is estimated from the same REML residual curves
that generate the plasmode errors). Both are thus much better than REML, worse than NCV in the
simulation and comparable to NCV in that plasmode comparison. Including the REML pilot fit, a pcre fit took `r f(min(time_ratio("PCRE", "synthetic")), 1)`--`r f(max(time_ratio("PCRE", "synthetic")), 0)` times as long as an NCV fit in the simulation
and `r f(min(time_ratio("PCRE", "plasmode")), 1)`--`r f(max(time_ratio("PCRE", "plasmode")), 0)` times as long on the plasmode data; a GLS fit took `r f(min(time_ratio("GLSfpc", "synthetic")), 1)`--`r f(max(time_ratio("GLSfpc", "synthetic")), 1)` and
`r f(min(time_ratio("GLSfpc", "plasmode")), 1)`--`r f(max(time_ratio("GLSfpc", "plasmode")), 1)` times as long (medians per setting). The GLS algorithm -- only applicable for Gaussian data -- is given in Supplement S3.2.

fig_coverage(fig1)

Bars: $\pm 2$ Monte Carlo SE. NCV + CL2 is discussed in @sec-res-tradeoff. Coverage for $\alpha(t)$ and $\gamma(t)$: @fig-s1-alpha-gamma in Appendix A.6; summary over all settings: @fig-tradeoff-summary. (b) Dependent errors (mean over the two processes). ## Intervals for the REML fit {#sec-res-intervals}

Model-based intervals undercover in every dependent setting and every family
(@fig-coverage): `r rng(cov_of(core_dep, "reml_model"))` for the mean and $\beta(s,t)$ with 100 curves. On a
four times denser grid ($D = 241$), their coverage of $\beta$ drops to `r rng(grid_cov("reml_model", 241))`.
REML + CL2 covers the mean and $\beta$ at `r rng(cov_of(core_dep, "reml_cl2"))` with 100 curves and stays at
`r rng(grid_cov("reml_cl2", 241))` for $\beta$ at $D = 241$. The same holds for $\alpha(t)$ and $\gamma(t)$ of
Gaussian and count responses, for scaled $t$, beta and negative-binomial responses, for the smooth-effect
model, for sign-changing and heteroskedastic errors, and for misregistered Gaussian curves (Supplement
S1.1--S1.3; misregistered Gaussian curves: mean and $\beta$ `r rng(warp_gau$coverage_mean)`). In the dependent main-factorial settings, REML + CL2's coverage is also
much more even over the grid: the lower tail for the mean and $\beta$ is `r rng(tq("reml_cl2", 100))` with 100 curves and `r rng(tq("reml_cl2", 40))`
with 40, against `r rng(tq("reml_model", 100))` for the model-based intervals with 100 curves.

Under independent errors with 100 curves, CL2 gives up `r rng_pp(iid_cost100)` of coverage against the model-based intervals for the mean and
$\beta$ (averaged over signal levels within each family). For binary responses with 40 curves at the default signal, it gives up
`r pp(max(bin40$cost))` for the mean, where the model-based intervals do not overcover (`r f(bin40$reml_cl2[which.max(bin40$cost)], 2)` against
`r f(bin40$reml_model[which.max(bin40$cost)], 2)`), and `r pp(abl_bin("alpha", "iid", "model") - abl_bin("alpha", "iid", "cl2e_b"))` and
`r pp(abl_bin("gamma", "iid", "model") - abl_bin("gamma", "iid", "cl2e_b"))` for $\alpha(t)$ and $\gamma(t)$ (Appendix A.6).

*Fewer curves.* With 40 curves, REML + CL2 covers the mean and $\beta$ at `r rng(cov_of(core_dep40, "reml_cl2"))`.
With 20 curves, it covers the mean, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ at `r rng(l20("reml_cl2"))` and $\alpha(t)$ at
`r rng(l20("reml_cl2", e = "alpha"))`. Satterthwaite degrees of freedom recover most of this shortfall
(@fig-satt): with 20 curves and the default signal, coverage of the mean, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ rises from
`r rng(sv("cov_z", 20))` to `r rng(sv("cov_satt", 20))`, at up to `r f(max(sv("wr", 20)), 2)` times the width;
with 100 curves, the change is small. The binary intercept stays short (`r f(sv("cov_satt", 20, e = "alpha", fam = "binomial"), 2)`
with 20 curves, `r f(satt_bin_alpha, 2)` with 40). The degrees of freedom are about a third of $G - 1$ for the mean,
$\beta$ and $\gamma$, and larger for $\alpha(t)$. In the extensions, they never lower coverage. There, with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, coverage stays below
`r f(LEVEL - ADEQUATE, 2)` in `r nrow(satx_low)` of `r n_satx` combinations of setting and estimand, all under misregistration or for binary
intercepts and scalar effects (Supplement S1.7).

*CL2 and CR1.* Under dependence and with the normal critical value, CL2 covers the mean and $\beta$
`r rng_pp(cr1_gain(40))` more than CR1 with the same allowance with 40 curves, at `r rng(cr1_wr(40), 1)` times its
width, and `r rng_pp(cr1_gain(100))` more with 100, at `r rng(cr1_wr(100), 2)` times (Appendix A.6). For fixed
smoothing parameters and a fixed basis, the two covariances agree to first order as the number of curves grows
(Appendix A.5). CR1 was not run with 20 or with more than 100 curves. The leverage adjustment costs a median of `r f(cl2_time, 1)` s per fit with 100 curves.

*Where CL2 falls short.* For binary responses, REML + CL2 covers the functional intercept and the scalar effect
at `r rng(ag_bin(TRUE))` under dependence and `r rng(ag_bin(FALSE))` under independent errors. Under independent errors with 40 curves, the
intercept's studentized error is centered but too spread out, which is compatible with a standard error that is too small, although local biases of
opposite sign are not excluded. Under dependence, it is also shifted (Supplement S1.4). Fixing the smoothing parameters at their typical value raises coverage of the binary
$\gamma(t)$ under independent errors from `r f(abl_bin("gamma", "iid", "cl2e_b"), 2)` to
`r f(abl_bin("gamma", "iid", "fix_cl2e_b"), 2)` and of $\alpha(t)$ under smooth errors from
`r f(abl_bin("alpha", "fpc", "cl2e_b"), 2)` to `r f(abl_bin("alpha", "fpc", "fix_cl2e_b"), 2)` (40 curves), so part of the
shortfall is likely due to uncounted smoothing-parameter variability; $\alpha(t)$ under independent errors stays at
`r f(abl_bin("alpha", "iid", "fix_cl2e_b"), 2)` (Appendix A.6, Supplement S1.4). With 20 curves and independent errors, every
interval undercovers binary $\alpha(t)$ and $\gamma(t)$, the model-based ones included
(`r rng(c(l20("reml_model", "independent", c("alpha", "gamma"), "binomial"), l20("reml_cl2", "independent", c("alpha", "gamma"), "binomial"), l20("ncv_cl2", "independent", c("alpha", "gamma"), "binomial")))`),
so this shortfall is not specific to the sandwich.

For misregistered counts, the working model for the mean is wrong: REML + CL2 covers the mean of misregistered
Poisson responses at `r rng(wp("reml_cl2"))` (model-based `r rng(wp("reml_model"))`).

## The trade-off for the coefficient surface {#sec-res-tradeoff}

In the simulation, REML's estimate of $\beta$ is noisy but has little bias, and CL2 measures its spread, so
its intervals cover. NCV's estimate has smaller error but more bias, beyond what the allowance
$\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e$ covers, so its narrower intervals cover less. A more accurate estimate therefore
need not give better coverage.

```{r}
#| label: fig-tradeoff-summary
#| fig-cap: "All simulation settings with dependent errors, 40 or 100 curves and a non-zero surface, per estimand and interval: median over settings of the relative error of the estimate, the grid-averaged coverage, the lower tail (5% quantile of pointwise coverage), the relative half-width and the detection rate, and the interval score relative to REML + CL2 (geometric mean over settings). Dashed: 0.95 for coverage, 1 for the ratio. The number of settings differs by estimand: $\\beta(s,t)$ and $\\alpha(t)$ are not scored in the smooth-effect model, and only the mean is scored for misregistered count and binary responses. Detection is defined for $\\beta(s,t)$ and $\\gamma(t)$ only. Values: Supplement S7."
#| fig-height: 4.3
fig_tradeoff_summary(trade_tab)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-tradeoff
#| fig-cap: "Coverage and detection rate for $\\beta(s,t)$ in all simulation settings with dependent errors, 40 or 100 curves and a non-zero surface (one symbol per setting and interval; panels by family on common axes; open symbols: rough truth; dashed: 0.95)."
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| fig-width: 5.4
fig_tradeoff(fig2b)
```

Under dependence, the median half-width of REML + CL2 for $\beta$ is
`r f(rs("beta", "dependent", "reml_cl2", "hw"), 1)` times the size of the effect, and it detects only
`r f(rs("beta", "dependent", "reml_cl2", "det"), 2)` of the grid points where the true value exceeds 25% of its
maximum (@fig-tradeoff-summary, @fig-tradeoff). Its intervals are
`r f(rs("beta", "dependent", "reml_cl2", "hw") / rs("beta", "dependent", "ncv_cl2", "hw"), 1)` times as wide as those of
NCV + CL2, which detects `r f(rs("beta", "dependent", "ncv_cl2", "det"), 2)` but covers less (median
`r f(rs("beta", "dependent", "ncv_cl2", "coverage"), 2)`, lower tail `r f(rs("beta", "dependent", "ncv_cl2", "q05"), 2)`). The
interval score of NCV + CL2 is `r f(scr("beta", "ncv_cl2"), 2)` times REML + CL2's: the score rewards its accurate,
narrow intervals more than it punishes the additional misses. We nevertheless do not recommend NCV + CL2 for
inference, because its coverage is too low on the real residual curves (@sec-plasmode).

In the simulation, the shortfall of NCV + CL2 is smoothing bias: subtracting the bias of the NCV estimate, estimated
from the replicates, raises its coverage from `r rng(nd("core", "coverage"))` to
`r rng(nd("core", "coverage_bias_elim"))` in the main factorial with 100 curves. NCV + CL2 covers less with 20 curves
and dependent errors (`r rng(l20("ncv_cl2", e = c("mean", "beta", "alpha", "gamma")))` for the four estimands), with a
rough truth (`r rng(rn("ncv_cl2"))`; REML + CL2: `r rng(rn("reml_cl2"))`) and for binary responses with 40 curves
(`r rng(bin40_ncv)`).

The trade-off grows with the basis: with the largest basis and smooth errors, REML + CL2's half-width for $\beta$
reaches `r rng(hwb("reml_cl2", "xlarge"), 0)` times the effect and its detection rate falls to
`r rng(hwb("reml_cl2", "xlarge", "detect"))`, while its coverage stays at `r rng(cov_bb("reml_cl2", "xlarge"))`.
Wrong-sign exclusions are rare for REML + CL2 (at most `r f(100 * rs("beta", "dependent", "reml_cl2", "wrong"), 1)`% of
the grid in any dependent setting).

For the mean, $\alpha(t)$ and $\gamma(t)$, the trade-off is mild: REML + CL2's intervals are wider than NCV + CL2's (mean:
`r f(rs("mean", "dependent", "reml_cl2", "hw") / rs("mean", "dependent", "ncv_cl2", "hw"), 1)` times), but they cover, the
estimates of $\alpha(t)$ and $\gamma(t)$ are about as accurate, and $\gamma(t)$ is detected at
`r f(rs("gamma", "dependent", "reml_cl2", "det"), 2)`.

The model-based intervals of pcre and GLS with an FPCA residual covariance show the trade-off from the other side.
In the `r n_cmp_dep` Gaussian main-factorial settings with dependent errors, they cover $\beta$ at
`r rng(c(cmq("pcre"), cmq("gls_fpc")))`, at `r rng(c(cmq("pcre", col = "wr"), cmq("gls_fpc", col = "wr")), 1)` times REML + CL2's width and
about half its interval score, but pcre's intervals cover the mean at only `r rng(cmq("pcre", "mean"))` and $\alpha(t)$ at
`r rng(cmq("pcre", "alpha"))`. On real residual curves, both cover $\beta$ at only
`r rng(c(cmp_cov("pcre", "plasmode"), cmp_cov("gls_fpc", "plasmode")))` (@sec-plasmode).

CL2 also applies to these fits: GLS whitens the data within curves, so curves stay independent clusters, and pcre + CL2 is
CL2 on the pcre fit (Supplement S3.2). Under dependent synthetic errors, GLS-FPCA + CL2 covers $\beta$ at
`r f(cav("gls_fpc_cl2", "dependent"), 2)`, at `r f(cav("gls_fpc_cl2", "dependent", "wr"), 1)` times REML + CL2's width, and
pcre + CL2 repairs pcre's intervals for $\alpha(t)$ (`r f(cav("pcre", "dependent", e = "alpha"), 2)` to
`r f(cav("pcre_cl2", "dependent", e = "alpha"), 2)`). On the real residual curves, GLS-FPCA + CL2 covers $\beta$ at
`r f(cav("gls_fpc_cl2", "plasmode"), 2)` (`r rng(ca_pm_app$v)` by dataset) and pcre + CL2 at `r f(cav("pcre_cl2", "plasmode"), 2)`, against
`r f(cav("reml_cl2", "plasmode"), 2)` for REML + CL2. GLS with the raw residual covariance fails with or without CL2
(`r f(cav("gls_raw_cl2", "dependent"), 2)` under dependent synthetic errors). Fits that smooth more thus estimate better (@sec-res-estimation),
and the sandwich repairs much, but not all, of their undercoverage.

## A zero coefficient surface {#sec-res-null}

With $\beta \equiv 0$, the share of grid points at which an interval excludes zero is the pointwise
false-positive rate, nominally 0.05 (@fig-null). Under smooth errors, it is `r rng(nl("reml_cl2"))` for REML + CL2
with the normal critical value and `r rng(nl("reml_cl2_satt"))` with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom, against
`r rng(nl("ncv_cl2"))` for NCV + CL2 and `r rng(c(nl("reml_model"), nl("ncv_model")))` for the model-based intervals of
either fit. Under independent errors, REML + CL2 has
`r rng(c(nl("reml_cl2", "iid", g = 100), nl("reml_cl2", "iid", "binomial", 40)))`, except
`r f(nl("reml_cl2", "iid", "gaussian", 40), 3)` for Gaussian responses with 40 curves (NCV + CL2:
`r f(nl("ncv_cl2", "iid", "gaussian", 40), 3)`). There, REML shrinks the surface to near the null space of its penalty in
most replicates, and in some of these the interval excludes zero over much of the grid, a known weakness of intervals for
terms shrunk to their null space [@MarraWood2012].

Under smooth errors, REML's estimate of the zero surface has `r rng(nl("reml_cl2", col = "rms_rel"), 1)` times the
root-mean-square size of the non-zero surface in the corresponding setting: spurious structure. NCV's estimate is
`r rng(nrr("fpc"), 0)` times smaller. Under independent errors, both are close to zero.

Pointwise intervals do not answer whether $\beta$ is zero everywhere: under smooth errors,
`r rng(nl("reml_cl2_satt", col = "any_excl"), 2)` of the replicates have at least one grid point where the Satterthwaite
interval excludes zero. That question needs simultaneous bands or global tests, which this study does not evaluate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-null
#| fig-cap: "Zero surface ($\\beta \\equiv 0$), default signal, by family, errors and number of curves $G$ (log scales). Left: pointwise false-positive rate of the model-based REML interval, REML + CL2 with the normal and the Satterthwaite critical value and NCV + CL2 (dashed: nominal 0.05). Right: root-mean-square size of the REML and NCV estimates relative to the non-zero surface of the corresponding setting (dotted: 1). Values: Supplement S1.8 and S7."
#| fig-height: 4
fig_null(SGN, ERR3)
```

## Other remedies {#sec-res-other}

We also evaluated the following constructions.

- *Intervals centered at the NCV estimate.* We tried widening by the NCV--REML difference, the NCV estimate with REML + CL2's half-width, a one-step bias correction of the NCV
  estimate and a cluster-robust term for the variability of the selected smoothing parameters, alone and combined. The combination is a frozen-map
  approximation: it propagates the smoothing-parameter term through the bias-correction map but ignores how that map changes with the smoothing
  parameters. In Gaussian settings, it covers $\beta$ at `r f(cbs("rbc_p_ijx", "core"), 2)` (smooth truths) and `r f(cbs("rbc_p_ijx", "rough_truth"), 2)` (rough truths), but none of these constructions held its level across the plasmode datasets (@sec-plasmode-results; Supplement S4.1).
- *mgcv's neighborhood covariance for NCV fits.* For curve blocks, the mgcv version used here returns the Bayesian
  $\mathbf V_p$ or, with `jackknife = TRUE`, essentially $\mathbf V_p - \mathbf V_e$; it computes this
  covariance correctly only for per-point neighborhoods. Computed correctly from the block fit, it is
  conservative in the simulation for $\beta$ (`r rng(jfs("jk_nei"))` with smooth errors and 100 curves, at about half of
  REML + CL2's width) and for Gaussian and Poisson responses, but it covers binary $\alpha(t)$ and $\gamma(t)$ at only
  `r rng(c(jf_bin("alpha"), jf_bin("gamma")))`. Over the combinations of truth and residual source on the six plasmode datasets with independent source curves, it
  undercovers $\beta$ (`r f(mean(jfp("jk_nei")), 2)` on average; NCV + CL2 `r f(mean(jfp("ncv_cl2")), 2)`,
  REML + CL2 `r f(mean(jfp("reml_cl2")), 2)`). Residual smoothing bias of the NCV estimate is a plausible
  contributor; variance and tail errors are not excluded (Supplement S4.2).
- *A smoothing-parameter uncertainty term for REML + CL2* raises coverage of $\beta$ by
  `r rng_pp(tapply(lc$gain, lc$G, mean))` without improving the interval score (Supplement S4.3).
- *An AR(1) working model* (`bam()` with AR(1) errors restarting at each curve, correlation profiled
  by the restricted-likelihood criterion; Appendix B.1) covers `r rng(ar1_main$coverage_mean)` on the
  nine plasmode datasets (Supplement S3.1).
- *The curve bootstrap* (resampling curves and refitting) covers `r rng(cmp_cov("boot_pct", "plasmode"))`
  on real residual curves, with intervals `r f(cmp_wr("boot_pct", "plasmode"), 1)` times as wide as
  REML + CL2's and a median of `r f(boot_time, 0)` s per analyzed dataset (Supplement S3.2).
- *Penalized functional GEE* [@LoewingerLevisCuiPereira2025], in the R package fastFGEE. Under dependent errors, it improves the surface over REML
  by less than NCV (mean squared error `r rng(fg_vs_ncv, 1)` times NCV's), and Wald intervals from its sandwich covariance cover $\beta$ at `r rng(fgb)`.
  Its interface offers a wild-bootstrap critical value for intercepts and scalar effects; we obtained it for the surface and fitted means from an internal
  routine. With an independence working correlation and its $t$ adjustment, the intervals for $\beta$ under dependence in the simulation were conservative and narrower than
  REML + CL2 with the Satterthwaite critical value: coverage `r rng(fg_beta_dep$coverage)` against `r rng(fg_beta_dep$cov_satt)`, lower tail
  `r rng(fg_beta_dep$pointwise_q05)` against `r rng(fg_beta_dep$q05_satt)`, at `r rng(fg_beta_dep$wr_satt)` times the width. On the `r nrow(fgp_all)` plasmode
  datasets with independent source curves (midpoint truth, REML residuals) and all subjects, they were again narrower (`r rng(fgp_all$wr_satt, 1)` times) and covered
  `r rng(fgp_all$coverage)` against `r rng(fgp_all$cov_satt)`, but on `r nrow(fgp_all_lowq)` of them their coverage was much less even (lower tail
  `r rng(fgp_all_lowq$pointwise_q05)` against `r rng(fgp_all_lowq$q05_satt)`). With 40 subjects, the $t$ adjustment often reached its floor of one degree of freedom
  and made them `r rng(fgp_40$wr_satt, 1)` times that width; without it, they covered down to `r f(min(fgp_40_not$coverage), 2)`, against
  `r rng(fgp_40_not$cov_satt)`. For fitted means under dependence, without the $t$ adjustment, intervals were narrower in the simulation with similar coverage
  (`r rng(fg_mean_dep$coverage)` against `r rng(fg_mean_dep$cov_satt)`, at `r rng(fg_mean_dep$wr_satt, 1)` times the width), but covered less on these plasmode datasets
  (`r rng(fgp_mean_not$coverage)` against `r rng(fgp_mean_not$cov_satt)`). Details, also for independent errors: Supplement S3.3.

# Plasmode study {#sec-plasmode}

## Design {#sec-plasmode-design}

A plasmode study simulates from real data with a known truth [@FranklinSchneeweissPolinskiRassen2014].
Each of nine datasets is fitted with the model in @eq-model by REML and by curve-blocked NCV. A fit's fitted
means serve as the truth: the *REML-fitted truth*, the *NCV-fitted truth*, and a *midpoint truth*
refitted with every smoothing parameter at the geometric mean of the two fits' values. A replicate
adds each subject's real residual curve, from the REML or the NCV fit, with a random sign (a *curve flip*) to
the truth at its own covariates. This keeps the covariates, the residual shapes and their within-curve
dependence, and makes the truth known. Because the signs are independent, the simulated errors are
independent across curves, and each subject's error takes only two values, plus or minus its
residual curve: the construction is a Rademacher wild cluster bootstrap around the fitted residuals,
not a model of new real curves. Its truths are exactly representable by the fitted model, so it
cannot evaluate misspecification of the mean.

In six datasets, the source curves are independent:
ECG-derived myocardial strain, atrial strain from a randomized trial, knee moments during running and
walking, the DTI tract profiles and an eight-lead ECG dataset. In three, the source curves are serially
or spatially dependent (monthly ocean profiles, weather stations, weekly electricity demand); their
simulated errors are still independent across curves, except in block-flip runs reported in the
supplement. The midpoint fit lies between the REML and NCV fits for every term on only
`r n_mid_interior` of the 9 datasets, and its surface is rougher than both on
`r paste(APP_LABELS[mid_above], collapse = ", ")`; it is a third smoothing level, not a compromise. The datasets have
`r rng(DS_TAB$G, 0)` curves on `r rng(DS_TAB$D, 0)` grid points, design effects of the residual
curves of `r rng(DS_TAB$DE, 0)` and functional covariates of rank `r rng(DS_TAB$rank_X, 0)`
(Appendix B.2). Each combination of dataset, truth and residual source is run with all subjects
and with 40, with `r n_rep` replicates; the mean is scored for a fixed set of 50 subjects.

## Results {#sec-plasmode-results}

```{r}
#| label: fig-plasmode-est
#| fig-cap: "Plasmode relative error of the REML and NCV estimates of $\\beta(s,t)$, all subjects, by dataset and truth source (median over replicates and the two residual sources; log scale; dotted: error as large as the effect)."
#| fig-height: 3.2
fig_plasmode_est(fig4)
```

*Estimation.* The median relative errors are `r rng(ptab$rel_reml_cl2, 1)` for REML and `r rng(ptab$rel_ncv_cl2, 1)` for
NCV across datasets (@fig-plasmode-est, @fig-plasmode-info). Weak identification of $\beta$ in directions the
functional covariate barely excites is a possible reason for their size (@sec-intro). Which fit is better depends on the
truth: NCV's relative error is `r rng(ptr("NCV"))` times REML's under the NCV-fitted truth, `r rng(ptr("MID"))` times
under the midpoint truth and `r rng(ptr("REML"))` times under the REML-fitted truth, where NCV is worse on
`r sum(ptr("REML") > 1)` of the 9 datasets. A fit used as truth is shaped like the selector that produced it, so the truth
source favors that selector; the simulation, whose truths come from neither fit, is the cleaner comparison, although
part of its gap reflects its smooth truths (@sec-res-estimation). For the mean, NCV's relative error is
`r rng(pm_mean_ratio$q)` times REML's per dataset.

```{r}
#| label: fig-plasmode
#| fig-cap: "Plasmode coverage of nominal 95% pointwise intervals for the mean and $\\beta(s,t)$, all subjects: mean over truth and residual sources (symbols) and their range (bars). Dashed: 0.95."
#| fig-height: 3.9
fig_plasmode(fig3)
```

*Intervals.* With curve flips, the simulated errors are independent across curves on all nine datasets, so CL2's
assumption holds on all of them. Model-based intervals cover
`r rng(c(pm("reml_model", c("mean", "beta")), pm("reml_model", c("mean", "beta"), "stress test")))` for the mean and
$\beta$. REML + CL2 covers the mean at `r rng(pm9("mean"))` on all nine datasets and $\beta$ at `r rng(others_beta$c)` on eight
(@fig-plasmode), but $\beta$ at only `r f(mean(wthr$coverage_mean), 2)` on the weather data, which combine few curves
(`r wds$G`), a functional covariate of rank `r wds$rank_X` and rough residuals.

REML + CL2's coverage of $\beta$ is below 0.95 in `r n_p_below` of `r n_p_all` combinations of dataset, truth, residual
source, number of subjects and construction variant; these combinations share data and are not independent
confirmations. Its standard error is somewhat smaller than the replicate spread of the estimate (median ratio
`r rng(cl2_sesd_p$s, 2)` per dataset), which is consistent with a standard error a little short, plus further error on some datasets.
With 40 subjects on the six datasets with independent source curves, REML + CL2 covers $\beta$ `r rng_pp(g40a("beta"))` below
nominal and the mean `r rng_pp(g40a("mean"))` below; on the weather data, it covers $\beta$ at `r rng(wthr40$coverage_mean)`.

With Satterthwaite degrees of freedom (Supplement S2.1), REML + CL2 covers $\beta$ at `r f(spm("satt", "all"), 2)` on average over
the nine datasets with all subjects and `r f(spm("satt", "40"), 2)` with 40 (normal critical value:
`r f(spm("z", "all"), 2)` and `r f(spm("z", "40"), 2)`), at `r f(spm("satt", "all", col = "wr"), 2)` and
`r f(spm("satt", "40", col = "wr"), 2)` times the width. It covers the mean, $\alpha(t)$ and $\gamma(t)$ at
`r rng(sapply(c("mean", "alpha", "gamma"), \(e) c(spm("satt", "all", e), spm("satt", "40", e))), 2)`. The weather surface
stays short (`r f(spa("satt", "all", apps = "aemet"), 2)` with all subjects, `r f(spa("satt", "40", apps = "aemet"), 2)` with 40). Adding
the smoothing-parameter uncertainty term and using the $t_{G-1}$ critical value helps about as much, with the weather
surface again short (Supplement S4.3).

On the six datasets with independent source curves, NCV + CL2 covers $\beta$ at `r rng(pm("ncv_cl2", "beta"))`, with lower
tails `r rng(pm("ncv_cl2", "beta", col = "q05_mean"))`, and loses up to `r pp(max(g40v("ncv_cl2", "beta")), 0)` with 40
subjects. Its standard error is short (median ratio to the replicate standard deviation `r rng(ncv_sesd$se_sd[ncv_sesd$role == "counted"], 2)` across
these datasets). A refit with the smoothing parameters fixed at their median restores it (`r rng(FX$se_sd[FX$role == "counted"], 2)`), but coverage then
still stays at `r rng(FX$cov[FX$role == "counted"])`. Fixing the smoothing parameters changes both the amount and the variability of smoothing, so
this is a diagnostic, not an exact decomposition; it suggests smoothing bias as the larger part (Supplement S4.1).

```{r}
#| label: fig-plasmode-info
#| fig-cap: "Plasmode study, $\\beta(s,t)$, all subjects, per dataset: median relative error of the REML and NCV estimates; coverage, detection rate; for REML + CL2 the lower tail (5% quantile of pointwise coverage) and the relative half-width; for NCV + CL2 the interval score relative to REML + CL2 (means, medians or geometric means over truth and residual sources). Gray segments join the two intervals of a dataset; log scales for relative error and half-width. Dashed: 0.95 for coverage, 1 for the ratio. Values: Supplement S7."
#| fig-height: 3.6
fig_plasmode_info(ptab)
```

*Informativeness.* As in the simulation, REML + CL2 is close to nominal but wide for $\beta$: its half-width is
`r rng(ptab$hw_reml_cl2, 1)` times the effect, and it detects `r rng(ptab$det_reml_cl2)` of the grid points where the true
value exceeds 25% of its maximum. NCV + CL2 detects more (`r rng(ptab$det_ncv_cl2)`) but does not hold its level, and here
its interval score is `r rng(ptab$score_ncv, 1)` times REML + CL2's (higher on `r sum(ptab$score_ncv > 1)` of the 9 datasets).

Intervals centered at the NCV estimate with a bias correction and a smoothing-parameter term (@sec-res-other) cover $\beta$ at
`r rng(cbv("rbc_p_ijx", "counted"))` on the six datasets with independent source curves, against
`r rng(rbv("reml_cl2", "counted"))` for REML + CL2, at `r rng(cbc$wr, 1)` times its width and with lower tails as low as
`r f(min(CB_P$coverage_q05[CB_P$arm == "rbc_p_ijx" & CB_P$estimand == "beta" & CB_P$role == "counted"]), 2)` in single
combinations. On the three datasets with dependent source curves, they cover `r rng(cbv("rbc_p_ijx", "stress test"))` (Supplement
S4.1). These comparisons are descriptive, on different replicate windows, without a paired measure of precision. The NCV
estimate with REML + CL2's half-width covers `r f(hyb_v("hybrid", "REML"), 2)` under the REML-fitted truth, but its lower tail is
`r f(hyb_v("hybrid", "REML", "pointwise_q05"), 2)`, against a lower tail of `r f(hyb_v("reml_cl2", "REML", "pointwise_q05"), 2)` for REML + CL2.

# Recommendations and software {#sec-recommend}

::: {.callout-note title="Recommendations for applied work with pffr()"}
1. **Assume within-curve dependence.** Expect REML to undersmooth coefficient surfaces, and do not use
   model-based intervals of the working-independence fit: they undercover, more so on dense grids
   (@sec-res-estimation, @sec-res-intervals).
2. **Shape of the surface: a fit that typically smooths more than REML.** By default, fit the same model with
   `method = "NCV"` and show its surface estimate as the description of the effect. The forthcoming
   refund releases then set one neighborhood per curve (per `cluster` if given); in earlier releases and in plain `gam()`,
   `method = "NCV"` alone leaves out single points, and the neighborhoods must be supplied through
   `nei`. NCV's gain in estimation also holds, more weakly, for smooth effects of scalar covariates that vary along $t$ (@sec-res-estimation).
   Do not attach the REML + CL2 band to NCV estimates, and do not use NCV + CL2 intervals for inference
   (@sec-res-tradeoff, @sec-plasmode-results). For the intercept, scalar effects and fitted means, REML + CL2 gives both the estimate and the
   intervals, with the exceptions in 5.

   NCV is not uniformly better: it was worse on some plasmode datasets under the REML-fitted truth, which favors REML
   (@sec-plasmode-results). Apart from misregistration, a small share of its fits under dependence have an unusually small smoothing parameter and a
   larger error, which convergence flags rarely reveal outside scaled-$t$ responses, although NCV still estimated the surface better than REML on
   nearly all of these replicates (@sec-res-estimation). When the surface was zero, its estimate stayed much closer to zero than REML's, which showed
   structure (@sec-res-null). For Gaussian responses, pcre and GLS with an FPCA residual covariance also estimated the surface much better than REML,
   but worse than NCV in the simulation and comparably to it in a plasmode comparison (@sec-res-estimation). If mgcv flags an NCV fit as not
   converged, as it usually did for scaled-$t$ responses, refitting from other starting smoothing parameters and comparing the
   criterion and the surface is a simple check (Appendix B.1); it was not evaluated as a procedure.
3. **Inference: REML + CL2 with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom.** Fit by REML and use the curve-clustered CL2
   covariance with the full block and the Satterthwaite critical value. This was evaluated for all four estimands in the
   main factorial at the default signal with 20, 40 and 100 curves, in all extensions and in the plasmode study. Under dependence, it was close to
   nominal for the mean, $\beta$ and $\gamma$ in the main factorial and for $\beta$ on average in the plasmode study, but not on one dataset with few curves and
   a low-rank covariate (@sec-res-intervals, @sec-plasmode-results); for further exceptions, see 5. The price is width, which is largest with few curves.
   The intervals for the surface are wide; report them as they are. fastFGEE's wild-bootstrap intervals for $\beta$, obtained from an internal routine, were conservative and narrower under dependence in the
   simulation, but we keep REML + CL2 because on most of the six plasmode datasets with independent source curves its pointwise coverage was more even, and it kept its coverage at
   40 subjects without the large widening of fastFGEE's $t$ adjustment (@sec-res-other). Only pointwise intervals were evaluated: a pointwise band answers "is there an effect, and
   where" poorly (@sec-plasmode-results) and "is $\beta$ zero everywhere" not at all, which needs simultaneous bands or
   global tests (@sec-res-null).
4. **Both goals: fit twice.** When the shape and error rates both matter, fit the model by NCV and by
   REML. The two fits differ only in how the smoothing parameters are chosen; @sec-res-tradeoff explains why they differ. In our Gaussian
   benchmark with 100 curves, an NCV fit took about `r f(tt("curve-blocked NCV fit", "A") / tt("REML fit", "A"), 0)` times as long as a REML fit (Appendix C). Take the surface from the NCV fit and
   disregard that fit's standard errors; take the intervals from the REML fit. Report them side by side, for example the NCV
   surface next to REML + CL2's map of grid points whose interval excludes zero, labeled as pointwise, not as a band around the
   NCV surface. Under a zero surface, most replicates show some excluded points (@sec-res-null); this display and
   disagreements between the two fits were not evaluated. If only fitted means, the intercept or scalar effects matter, one REML
   fit with these intervals is enough, with the exceptions in 5.
5. **Exceptions.** Treat intervals for the intercept and scalar effects of binary responses and for
   misregistered counts as approximate; they undercover, also with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom (@sec-res-intervals).
6. **Few curves.** Use the Satterthwaite critical value. With 20 curves and dependent errors in the main factorial, it brought the mean, $\beta$ and $\gamma$
   close to nominal, but not binary intercepts (@sec-res-intervals); with 20 curves and independent errors, every interval undercovered binary intercepts and
   scalar effects. Nothing below 20 curves, or with 20 curves outside the main factorial, was evaluated; treat intervals there as approximate. On the weather
   data with `r n_blocks_weather` independent blocks and in a function-on-scalar design with 25 subjects, block- and subject-clustered CL2 covered below
   nominal (Supplement S2.3, S3.3).
7. **Several curves per subject.** Cluster by subject (`cluster =`); in a function-on-scalar design with five curves per subject,
   this was close to nominal with 100 or 500 subjects (Supplement S3.3). It leaves fewer clusters and does not address dependence
   between subjects. With `method = "NCV"`, the same argument gives subject neighborhoods, which were not evaluated.
8. **Basis and identification.** Refit with a richer basis and compare. A richer basis protects
   against approximation bias but widens REML + CL2's intervals (@sec-res-tradeoff). It does not help where the
   functional covariate carries little information about a direction of the surface: the surface is
   then weakly identified [@ScheiplGreven2016]. Refrain from interpreting the surface's shape when
   the estimate or its interval changes substantially with the basis, or when the covariate's
   principal components leave the relevant directions poorly covered given the penalty's null
   space; agreement between two penalized fits does not certify identification. Fitted means or
   well-supported contrasts are then safer targets, though not protected against misspecification (Supplement S5).
9. **Covariates with few principal components.** If the functional covariate's variation is
   concentrated in a few principal components, an `ffpc()` term with a small number of components
   can replace `ff()`. With the low-rank covariate of one synthetic setting, the `r ffv(FFPC_LR, "p095", col = "K_median")` components that explain 95% of its variance
   estimated $\beta$ about as well as NCV with `ff()` and much better than REML with `ff()`; their CL2 intervals with the normal critical value covered
   `r f(ffv(FFPC_LR, "p095", col = "coverage"), 2)` (`r f(ffv(FFPC_LR, "k5", col = "coverage"), 2)` with five components; Supplement S1.9). For
   covariates with a richer spectrum, keep `ff()`: few components truncate the surface and the
   intervals undercover, and a high variance-explained threshold, such as 0.99 (the default of current refund releases),
   gives unstable, very noisy estimates, as is known for functional principal component regression, an ill-posed problem [@HallHorowitz2007; @ReissOgden2007].
:::

Forthcoming releases of refund (version X.Y or later) and mgcv (version X.Y or later) will
implement these recommendations, with REML + CL2 and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom as the default
intervals of `pffr()` fits, and contain the corrections found in this study, among them those of
mgcv's covariances for NCV fits (Supplement S4.2). Supplement S6 gives example code, the software
used in the study and a reproduction route.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

Under within-curve dependence, the working-independence REML fit of a penalized function-on-function
regression gives an undersmoothed, noisy estimate of the coefficient surface and model-based intervals
that are far too narrow. A fit that typically smooths more, by default curve-blocked NCV, improves the estimate
but not the intervals. A curve-clustered sandwich with a leverage adjustment for the penalized
hat and Satterthwaite degrees of freedom brings the intervals close to nominal for most estimands of Gaussian, count
and binary responses in the simulation, down to 20 curves, and for the surface on eight of the nine
plasmode datasets, but it cannot improve the estimate it is centered on. The two remedies thus show the
undersmoothing-versus-bias-correction tension of nonparametric inference
[@Hall1992; @CalonicoCattaneoFarrell2018], here produced by the dependence, hence our recommendation to fit twice when the surface matters. Intermediate amounts of smoothing between REML and NCV, global
tests of $\beta \equiv 0$ and simultaneous bands are the natural next steps; they were not studied
here. The evidence has the following limits.

- *Binary responses.* REML + CL2 undercovers intercepts and scalar effects of binary responses, also
  under independent errors and with Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. The diagnostics are compatible with a standard error
  that is too small for these terms, partly through smoothing-parameter variability; local bias is not excluded. Every
  interval centered at the NCV estimate undercovers for binary responses (Supplement S4.1).
- *Misregistration.* When curves are observed on their own clocks, the observed-clock mean of a
  count response is not a generalized linear predictor, and no method covers it; for Gaussian
  responses, REML + CL2 is unaffected.
- *Design.* The synthetic design has 20 curves only in the main factorial, a zero surface only for
  Gaussian and binary responses with independent and smooth errors, one empirically derived smooth
  error kernel (from the DTI data) beside parametric kernels, and first-order difference penalties
  throughout.
- *Truths outside the spline space.* All synthetic truths in the main study are representable. For
  a truth with components the covariates barely excite and the default basis cannot represent
  (Supplement S5), REML + CL2 covers $\beta$ at only `r rng(msv("T2", "default", "reml_cl2", err = "fpc"))`
  under smooth errors and `r f(msv("T2", "default", "reml_cl2", err = "iid"), 2)` under independent
  errors. A basis with four times finer knot spacing restores `r rng(msv("T2", "xlarge", "reml_cl2", err = "fpc"))`
  under smooth errors, at the price of wider intervals, but only
  `r f(msv("T2", "xlarge", "reml_cl2", err = "iid"), 2)` under independent errors; NCV + CL2 stays short
  even then. These coverages refer to the exact truth, which mixes approximation bias with weak identification.
- *Plasmode study.* Fits used as truths favor their own selector, the errors are sign-flipped
  fitted residuals with independent signs across curves, the truths are representable by the model,
  and all nine datasets are Gaussian and were chosen, not sampled.
- *Intervals around the NCV estimate.* Their shortfall is smoothing bias in the simulation; on the
  plasmode data, the diagnostics suggest smoothing bias and the variability of the selected smoothing
  parameters, but fixing the smoothing parameters changes both. Neither a one-step bias correction nor
  a variance term for the smoothing parameters, nor their combination as a frozen-map approximation, gave a narrower calibrated interval in the
  plasmode study. Calibrated intervals after data-driven heavier smoothing remain open for the NCV fit. A wild-bootstrap critical value around fastFGEE's fit gave conservative intervals for $\beta$, narrower than REML + CL2 with the Satterthwaite critical
  value, under dependence in the simulation. On most of the plasmode datasets with independent source curves, its coverage was less even with all subjects, and with 40 subjects its
  intervals were very wide with the $t$ adjustment and undercovered without it. That fit's mean squared error for $\beta$ under dependence in the simulation is still
  `r rng(fg_vs_ncv, 1)` times NCV's (@sec-res-other).

# Code and data availability {.unnumbered}

Code and summary files are at <https://github.com/fabian-s/fof-inf>; the tables and figures of this paper
and its supplement are computed from those summary files. The per-replicate records are at
<https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23916388>. Records of the two cardiology datasets are patient and volunteer
data and are not shared; only aggregate results are available for them. The other datasets are public
(Appendix B.2).
